transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2028-04-17
Start: 15:00 PDT
Duration: 62 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Samir (Redwood SE), Lena (Redwood Product), Aisha (Head of Platform - Northern Lighting), Diego (ML Eng), Tom (CTO)

--- Auto Summary (auto-gen, may be rough) ---
Maya: quick agenda, show Optimize console prefetch recommendations; Samir: demo sandbox, cost model; customer: heavy focus on latency SLO (85-95th pctl) and data residency; agreed on sandbox run.

00:00:12 Maya: okay cool good morning team, um welcome everyone, this is Maya from Redwood, today we want to run through our opt console prefetch and batching playbook and then get aligned on a sandbox to validate hit rates with your session traces
00:00:26 Aisha: thanks Maya, we have Diego and Tom on, we're looking at pretty strict latency SLOs for the new conversational lighting assistant, 95th under 380ms ideally and cost needs to hit our ops budget
00:00:45 Samir: yep totally, we'll show how prefetch (we sometimes call it lookahead or prefix KV) plus batching can reduce token cost while keeping 95/99 latency in control. quick note, our runtime has continuous batching + kv cache that can be tuned per route
00:01:10 Diego: quick question, when you say prefetch are you actually running speculative generation and storing in the KV cache, or it's more of a prefix lookup?
00:01:26 Samir: good q — it's not generating future tokens blindly, it's prefetching model key/value states for likely next prefixes based on heuristics and session history. sometimes customers call it lookahead or pre-warming the KV; i might say prefetch and prefix-cache interchangeably in the demo so apologies
00:01:52 Tom: is that safe from a data retention POV? we can't send PII offsite and we'd prefer the private deployment route if possible
00:02:10 Maya: yes we covered deployment options in the intro — for private we provide the control plane in your VPC and all logs can be turned off or routed to your KMS, Samir can show the config in the console later
00:02:28 Lena: also pointing out that Optimize suggests quantization + smaller model variants as another lever but today we'll stick to batching/prefetch since their quality budget is tight
00:02:45 Samir: jumping into the console — loading the prefetch panel (screen share) — here's the cost model. we start with their qps and session length histogram. i mocked a few buckets based on the notes you shared.
00:03:10 Samir: timestamp: 03:10. so first tradeoff: prefetch window size (how many tokens ahead we warm). small window = modest hit-rate improvement but low extra compute; large window = better hit-rate but more wasted tokens if user deviates
00:03:44 Diego: can you quantify "modest"? ballpark numbers help us decide
00:03:52 Samir: sure — with our sample workloads, a 16-token lookahead improved prefix hit-rate from ~25% to ~46% for conversational turn-restoration; cost per request increased by ~6% compute but overall per-token billing fell by ~18% because batching amortized the overhead
00:04:18 Maya: and that 18% is sensitive to concurrency and batch sizing — if you have very low concurrency the batching benefits shrink
00:04:30 Aisha: our peak concurrency is about 120 active sessions per minute globally, typical median is 18, we have bursts at 220; does that map to your example?
00:04:45 Samir: that's a good range — our simulator takes qps + session histogram. i'll flag that bursts to 220 means we get better batching at peaks, but you need to keep tail latency controls (we can set max batch latency).
00:05:06 Tom: how do you handle timeouts if a batch is waiting to fill? we can't let a user sit longer than their 95th SLO
00:05:18 Samir: the runtime supports continuous batching with an adjustable max-wait (10ms-200ms). also we offer a split policy: small-requests fast-lane where latency-critical routes get prioritized and small batch sizes are used, while background routes batch more aggressively
00:05:40 Diego: okay interesting. what's the cost delta between hosted and dedicated if we need the private network?
00:05:52 Maya: depends on commit size; rough rule: hosted is pay-as-you-go per token and cheaper for spikey usage, dedicated is a reserved pool with lower per-token ops but an uptime/commit fee. we'll send specific numbers after we see your usage and run the sandbox
00:06:10 Samir: demo: switching to sim tab — here's the hit-rate sensitivity chart. see the purple curve — small changes in lookahead window change hit rate non-linearly, that's because common prefixes across sessions amplify returns
00:06:35 Samir: also pointing out cold start behavior — first request per session won't hit cache, so sessionization matters (sticky session affinity vs pure stateless). you told us you keep session ids for 24h?
00:06:50 Aisha: yes 24h retention on session IDs, but we purge content nightly. can the prefix cache be keyed to session id only and not persist full text?
00:07:02 Samir: absolutely. you can persist KV states with redacted context and only store key/value tensors, not raw text. also we support TTLs on cache entries — we recommend 2–6 hours for chat agents depending on convo drift
00:07:20 Diego: what about security — are those tensors encrypted at rest and in transit?
00:07:26 Maya: yes encrypted in transit and at rest; for private deployments you can plug in your KMS/HSM; for hosted we manage keys but offer customer-managed keys as an option
00:07:40 Aisha: great. can you walk through a concrete worked example with our 90th percentile session length?
00:07:47 Samir: sure — let me load a scenario: baseline -> no prefetch, batch size policy default (max 8, max-wait 50ms), cost per 1k requests x; then scenario B -> lookahead 12 tokens, batch target 16 with max-wait 30ms, cost change y.
00:08:15 Samir: in our mock, scenario B reduces effective per-request billed tokens by 21% because many tokens are served from cached KV states — that yields big savings especially on long-turn conversations
00:08:33 Tom: do you have examples where prefetch backfires? we worry about hallucination amplification or wasted compute if users change direction
00:08:43 Samir: yes — if your conversational flow has high branching (users often take new directions) then larger lookaheads produce wasted warmed states. our console shows a "waste metric" overlay — you'd pick a conservative window or pair prefetch with a small alpha that decays warm states if action diverges
00:09:05 Diego: how do we measure divergence? is it based on edit distance or token overlap?
00:09:11 Samir: heuristic currently is prefix overlap and token-level similarity; we're iterating on semantic similarity metrics but core is token prefix match for now
00:09:22 Maya: quick interjection on pricing model — remember billing is per token served, warming costs are computed as extra tokens generated by prefetch but can be offset when warmed tokens are re-used in subsequent requests
00:09:34 Aisha: ok so we need the sandbox to see real hit-rate with our queries. what's the data requirement — do you need raw text?
00:09:45 Samir: only session_id, timestamp, tokenized turn boundaries, and anonymized text. ideally 30 days of sample or a 90-day compressed histogram. you can strip PII before sharing
00:09:58 Aisha: we'll redact and provide 30 days to start
00:10:06 Samir: great, for sandbox we'll run three runs: conservative (lookahead 8), baseline (no prefetch), aggressive (lookahead 20) and capture hit-rate, wasted tokens, tail latency. i can include pre- and post- batching adjustments
00:10:24 Lena: also worth noting graph on the console shows concurrency sensitivity — if you enable session affinity the effective hit-rate improves because consecutive requests from same session hit the warmed KV
00:10:36 Diego: we do have session affinity at the app layer but it occasionally breaks with mobile clients; can the runtime rehydrate from a secondary cache?
00:10:47 Samir: yes we have a fallback policy to rehydrate from a persistent prefix store; it's slightly higher latency but keeps quality consistent. also routing fallback to a smaller model variant if the large model is unavailable
00:11:05 Tom: you mentioned model variants — do you recommend quantized LMs for this workload?
00:11:11 Lena: if quality doesn't regress, 4-bit quantization with a tuned kernel often saves 30–40% in compute. optimize will flag quality regressions using your eval prompts before recommending it
00:11:25 Aisha: delightful. for the sandbox, what's the expected time to get results?
00:11:30 Samir: once we get data, 3–5 business days to run the three scenarios and return a cost/hit-rate report plus config suggestions.
00:11:40 Maya: and then we'll set a follow-up to review results and decide between hosted pilot vs Dedicated commit for production
00:11:52 Diego: small nit — is the console metric "waste" inclusive of batching overhead or only prefetch wasted tokens?
00:11:59 Samir: it's both, we break the chart down by source: warmed-but-unused tokens, batching-overhead tokens, and model-variant fallbacks; you can export the spreadsheet for deeper analysis
00:12:15 Tom: any integration work for our auth / SSO? we need SAML and SCIM provisioning for teams
00:12:23 Maya: yes SAML + SCIM supported for Hosted and Dedicated console; for Private we coordinate with your infra team for SSO cert exchange. we'll attach the SSO integration guide in the follow-up email
00:12:38 Aisha: perfect. last question on observability — do you expose token-level traces per request? we need to tie cost back to business metrics
00:12:47 Lena: yes, per-route token breakdowns, KV hit attribution, and latency percentiles. retention settings are configurable and can be integrated with your SIEM if needed
00:12:58 Diego: cool. any red flags around regulatory compliance? we operate in EU and US
00:13:05 Maya: we have EU regions, data residency controls, SOC2 and ISO certifications available; for regulated customers we recommend Private with customer-managed keys
00:13:17 Samir: wrapping up the demo, i'll jot the recommended knobs: lookahead 8–12 tokens initially, batch target 12–16, max-wait 30–50ms, TTL 4h, session affinity enabled where possible. we'll tune after sandbox
00:13:38 Maya: recap — action items: get anonymized traces, run three sandbox scenarios, send pricing and SSO docs. anyone object?
00:13:50 Aisha: sounds good. Diego will lead the trace export. Tom will review security docs.
00:13:58 Maya: perfect, we'll aim for results by 2028-04-24. thanks everyone, we'll follow up with calendar invite for the review session
00:14:08 Tom: thanks team bye
